y-m-26-03.title: Wetin change as we learn more about diagonals?
y-m-26-03.topic: Properties of quadrilateral diagonals and identify quadrilaterals
y-m-26-03.goal: Explain, connecting to conditions, how your judgment that a quadrilateral na rectangle or square change as information about diagonals come one by one; use examples you make yourself to confirm say the first information alone no enough.
y-m-26-03.material: The two diagonals of quadrilateral ABCD na AC and BD. Rectangle na quadrilateral with all 4 angles right angles; rhombus get all 4 sides same length; square get all 4 angles right and all 4 sides same length. Assume you already know “a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other na parallelogram”. All quadrilaterals here na convex (no part bend inward).
y-m-26-03.thinking.0: Judge from partial information and revise when new info arrive
y-m-26-03.thinking.1: Work out if the converse (reverse statement) true
y-m-26-03.prereq.0: Wetin parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square mean, and their diagonal properties (Grade 8 level)
y-m-26-03.prereq.1: One parallelogram condition: “the two diagonals bisect each other”
y-m-26-03.prereq.2: Distance between 2 points on coordinate plane
y-m-26-03.s.s1.prompt: For quadrilateral ABCD, information about diagonal AC and BD go show one piece at a time. Every time, judge “fit we call am rectangle?” (No figure.)
y-m-26-03.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite each information as one property of the quadrilateral diagonals, and compare with diagonal properties of rectangle, parallelogram, and rhombus.

y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we call quadrilateral ABCD a rectangle?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Some quadrilaterals with equal diagonals no be rectangles (for example, an isosceles trapezoid). So this information alone no make us sure na rectangle. Look at the next information and change your judgment if needed.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Na rectangle, because rectangle diagonals equal
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: “If e rectangle, the diagonals equal” and “if diagonals equal, e rectangle” point in different directions. We must check separately if the reverse statement true too.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: You no fit claim say na rectangle. Some quadrilaterals no be rectangles even if the diagonals equal
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You fit draw quadrilateral with only the diagonal lengths equal. If even one dey, you no fit claim am.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: E no be rectangle, because nobody say the diagonals bisect each other
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: E might be rectangle. “Nobody say dem bisect each other” different from “dem no bisect each other”.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Information no enough, so we no fit tell now. E might or might not be rectangle
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.info: New information: both diagonals bisect each other. (If dem meet at O, then AO=CO and BO=DO.) The earlier information AC=BD still holds.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Can we call quadrilateral ABCD a rectangle now?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.after: If diagonals bisect each other, the quadrilateral na parallelogram. In parallelogram ABCD, compare triangles ABD and DCA: AB=DC, AD=DA (common), BD=CA, so dem congruent (SSS), and ∠A=∠D. Since AB ∥ DC, ∠A+∠D=180°, so ∠A=∠D=90°. So e na rectangle.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: We only know say na parallelogram; we still no know if na rectangle
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Correct, e na parallelogram. But you fit still use the “AC=BD” information we know from the start. Wetin happen if you use both pieces of information together?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: E no be rectangle, na rhombus
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: For rhombus, we need information say all 4 sides equal. So far we get no information about side lengths.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Na rectangle. Na parallelogram with diagonals equal, so all 4 angles become equal
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Na square, because the diagonals bisect each other
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: For square, we still need information say all 4 sides equal. Bisecting alone only tell us say na parallelogram.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Last thing we learn: both diagonals meet at right angle. (AC ⊥ BD)
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: If we combine am with all earlier information, what be the most detailed name for ABCD?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.after: For quadrilateral where diagonals bisect each other, if dem meet at right angle, na rhombus (4 equal sides). E already be rectangle, so all 4 angles right and all 4 sides equal; therefore na square. “Rectangle” from the earlier step still correct, but the new information make the name more exact.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: “Rhombus” no be wrong too, because the diagonals bisect and perpendicular. But if you combine am with the earlier information say na rectangle, there be more exact name.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Calling am rectangle no be wrong. But you no use the new “perpendicular” information. Wetin parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals be?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Na parallelogram but no be rectangle
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You learn from the earlier step say na rectangle. New information no fit cancel earlier conclusion.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.reflect: Think why the first information (diagonal lengths equal) alone no make you sure say na rectangle, wetin the second add, and if the last one change or add to the earlier conclusion.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.prompt: Make we check ourselves say if we only know the first information (AC=BD), e fit still no be rectangle. Put A(0, 0) and B(6, 0), then make 2 different convex quadrilaterals ABCD where diagonals AC and BD equal length and dem no be parallelograms. (Coordinates of C and D)

y-m-26-03.s.s2.explain: For example, if C(5, 3) and D(1, 3), AC²=34 and BD²=25+9=34 (isosceles trapezoid). If C(4, 3) and D(3, 4), AC=BD=5 but no two sides parallel. Both get equal diagonals but no be rectangles. So diagonal lengths alone no tell us for sure.

y-m-26-01.title: If you know two sides and one angle, one triangle don determine?
y-m-26-01.topic: Triangle congruence conditions (two sides and one angle)
y-m-26-01.goal: Make counterexamples yourself to show the claim “two sides and one angle equal” no always work, depending on where the angle dey; then judge what else we need to be sure the triangles congruent.
y-m-26-01.material:
Jihu talk, “For triangle ABC and triangle DEF, if AC=DF=10cm, BC=EF=6.5cm, and ∠A=∠D, then both triangles congruent!”

So we fit test am, I put triangle ABC on coordinate plane (one square na 1cm). A na origin (0, 0), and C na (8, 6). Then AC=10cm. B na point on x-axis, to the right of A (its x-coordinate positive). ∠A na the angle formed by segment AB on x-axis and segment AC. We fit place triangle DEF the same way, so AC=DF and ∠A=∠D. Now find point B wey make BC=6.5cm.
y-m-26-01.thinking.0: Read the claim conditions (where the angle dey?)
y-m-26-01.thinking.2: Judge whether information enough and find what else we need

y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.a: SAS only apply when the angle between the two sides equal. For this problem, ∠A dey between which of sides AC and BC?

y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.b: Na attitude wey consider where the angle dey too, and try test the judgment.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.o.c: Dem no congruent. Two sides and one angle no fit ever determine one triangle
y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.c: The problem na the word “ever”. If two sides and the angle between dem dey given, the triangle determine (SAS). Think where the angle dey.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.o.d: Before I see picture, I no fit talk if dem congruent or not
y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.d: The conditions dey as numbers, so you fit test am without picture. Make one yourself with coordinates or sketch.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.explain: Jihu shorten the condition to “two sides and one angle”. Here ∠A no dey between the given sides AC and BC. The result fit change depending on angle position, so make we test am yourself next.

y-m-26-01.s.s2.explain: If B=(5.5, 0), then AB=5.5cm; if B=(10.5, 0), then AB=10.5cm. For both triangles AC=10cm, BC=6.5cm, and ∠A same, but AB different, so dem no congruent. Jihu claim get counterexample: this case where e no work.

y-m-26-02.title: Wetin the problem be for this proof?
y-m-26-02.topic: Properties of isosceles triangles and mistake in a proof
y-m-26-02.goal: Find the mistake of using the conclusion we need to prove as evidence, and judge say we fit fix am in different ways to correctly meet a congruence condition.
y-m-26-02.material: Seohyeon wan prove, “For triangle ABC, if AB=AC, then ∠B=∠C.” AB=AC na assumption, and ∠B=∠C na conclusion to prove. Below na the proof Seohyeon write. Read am and separate the assumption from conclusion. Point M dey on side BC. (No figure dey. Imagine triangle ABC with a line from vertex A down to side BC.)
y-m-26-02.thinking.0: Separate proof lines into assumption/conclusion to find the mistake
y-m-26-02.thinking.1: Compare different correct ways to fix am
y-m-26-02.prereq.0: Wetin isosceles triangle mean (triangle with 2 equal sides)
y-m-26-02.prereq.1: Triangle congruence conditions SSS, SAS, and right-triangle condition RHS
y-m-26-02.s.s1.prompt: Seohyeon write the following to prove “the two base angles of an isosceles triangle equal”. Choose the line wey hard to accept as proof.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, mark if e use “wetin dem give (assumption)” or “wetin we must prove (conclusion)”.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.hint.1: Sort the 3 things in line 3: assumption, result from earlier line, or wetin we must prove.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.1: Make M the midpoint of side BC and draw AM. Then BM=CM.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.2: For triangles ABM and ACM, AB=AC, ∠B=∠C (base angles of isosceles triangle), and AM common.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.3: So triangles ABM and ACM congruent.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.4: In congruent triangles, matching angles equal, so ∠B=∠C.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 already write ∠B=∠C as if na fact. That na the conclusion the proof need show. So line 4 congruence get no basis either (AB, ∠B, AM no be two sides and included angle), and line 5 just repeat the claim we start with.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.prompt: You wan fix Seohyeon proof. When you change how line 3 show congruence, choose all the ways wey make the proof correct.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.hint.0: For each method, check if the 3 things we use all be assumptions or come directly from how M choose.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check if the form match a congruence condition (SSS, SAS, RHS). Check too if any option use conclusion ∠B=∠C.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.a: Choose M as the foot of perpendicular from A to BC, then compare with AB=AC, AM common, ∠AMB=∠AMC=90°
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.b: Write ∠B=∠C and add say e correct because e look so in the picture
y-m-26-02.s.s2.r.b: The way e look in a picture no be proof. A proof show the reason wey make e look so.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.c: Choose M where the angle bisector of ∠A meet BC, then compare with AB=AC, ∠BAM=∠CAM, AM common
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.d: Write say triangles ABM and ACM congruent because their areas equal, then say corresponding angles equal
y-m-26-02.s.s2.r.d: Even if areas equal, the shapes fit different (for example, rectangles with different width and height). Equal area alone no make dem congruent.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.e: Choose M as midpoint of BC, then compare with AB=AC, BM=CM, AM common
y-m-26-02.s.s2.explain: e congruent because all 3 sides equal (SSS), c because two sides and included angle equal (SAS), and a because hypotenuse and another side of right triangle equal (RHS). None of the methods write ∠B=∠C first; dem get ∠B=∠C from congruence.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.prompt: Write message to Seohyeon. Say why the original proof no show “the base angles equal”, and explain how to fix am with one method above.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write one sentence to say which of the 3 things in line 3 na wetin we need prove.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one method from the options, write the 3 things e use, and check if dem match the name of a congruence condition.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Your writing make clear “wetin we don use and which line we use am”?
y-m-26-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: For the method you choose, you use ∠B=∠C only as the conclusion?
y-m-26-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: For your method, all 3 things in the congruence condition given, or come from how you choose point M?
y-m-26-02.s.s3.model.0: Line 3 already use ∠B=∠C. Na the conclusion we must prove, so e no fit serve as reason. You fit fix am using SSS congruence: assumption AB=AC, BM=CM because M midpoint, and AM common.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.model.1: It use ∠B=∠C, the thing we need prove, as reason for congruence first, so the proof go round in circle. If you choose M where angle bisector of ∠A meet BC, then use SAS with AB=AC, ∠BAM=∠CAM, and AM common, you no need assume ∠B=∠C first.

y-m-26-05.title: Can we make many triangles with area 12?
y-m-26-05.topic: Areas of triangles between parallel lines
y-m-26-05.goal: Understand say for triangles with same base to get same area, dem need same height; find different points wey satisfy area and angle conditions together, and explain why.
y-m-26-05.material: For coordinate plane, one square na 1cm. Points A(0, 0) and B(6, 0), and P dey above x-axis. Find point P wey make area of triangle ABP=12cm², and P coordinates all whole numbers.
y-m-26-05.thinking.0: Find different solutions wey satisfy conditions together
y-m-26-05.thinking.1: Understand the place (shape) where the points lie
y-m-26-05.prereq.0: Triangle area = base × height ÷ 2 (Grade 5 elementary level)
y-m-26-05.prereq.1: Position of points on coordinate plane, and acute, right, obtuse angles
y-m-26-05.prereq.2: If two lines parallel, distance between dem constant (distance between parallel lines)
y-m-26-05.s.s1.prompt: Coordinate plane get A(0, 0) and B(6, 0). You want P above x-axis and triangle ABP area=12cm². What shape go appear if you gather all possible P points? (One square na 1cm.)
y-m-26-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think how high the height must be for area 12, if AB na base of triangle ABP.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.hint.1: When you move P up or down perpendicular to AB, think which directions you fit move and keep the same height.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.a: Points on a circle with same distance from A
y-m-26-05.s.s1.r.a: Even if points on circle same distance from A, their distance from AB (the height) fit change.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.b: Only one point. Once area fixed at 12, P must be just one point
y-m-26-05.s.s1.r.b: Same base and same area mean same height. E only get one point with same height?
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.c: Points on a line through midpoint of AB and perpendicular to AB
y-m-26-05.s.s1.r.c: Points on this line get different distances from AB, so heights differ. Their areas no go be same.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.d: Points on line parallel to AB and 4cm away from AB
y-m-26-05.s.s1.explain: Base AB=6cm same, so for area 12cm², height must be 12×2÷6=4cm. All points 4cm from AB dey on line parallel to AB (y=4).
y-m-26-05.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different points P wey make triangle ABP area 12cm² and all 3 angles acute (below 90°). P coordinates must be whole numbers.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.hint.0: Among points on the line you find before, change x-coordinate one at a time and check if all angles acute.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.hint.1: Draw what happen to angles at A and B when x-coordinate too small or too big.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.ok.c1: P na point with whole-number coordinates above x-axis.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.fail.c1: P must dey above x-axis (y>0) and get whole-number coordinates.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Area of triangle ABP no be 12cm². Check base AB and height again.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.fail.c3: One of the 3 angles right or obtuse. Check angles at A, B, P one by one.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.explain: If P=(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4), (4, 4), (5, 4), all get height 4cm so area na 12. If x-coordinate na 0 or 6, angle at A or B right; outside those, one angle obtuse. So these 5 na the only integer points. Point (3, 4) give isosceles triangle, and the rest get different shapes.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare the points you find. Explain why areas same even if triangle shapes different, and how the acute-angle condition limit where points fit be.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the y-coordinates of the points and say which line dem dey on.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Draw the degree sizes of angles at A and B when P x-coordinate na 0 and when e na 6.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You explain say areas same because “base same and height same too”?
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You use angles to explain why x-coordinate 0, 6, or outside no work?
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.model.0: The points dey on a line parallel to AB; if AB na base, all heights na same 4 and base na same 6, so areas all 12. If x-coordinate na 0 or 6, angle at A or B right; if under 0 or pass 6, one angle obtuse, so only 1 to 5 work.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.model.1: Base AB na 6 and height same 4, so even if shapes different, areas same. All angles must acute, so P no fit directly above A or B or outside dem; x-coordinate must be between 0 and 6.
